There are a lot of ways. One of the most basic is that source of incomes for the wealthy are not the same as for the rest of us. Capital gains are one example. For instance the 6 Waltons currently receive a check of more than $3 billion a year in dividends. These dividends are already taxed at an unreasonably low rate such that they pay 20% on their $3 billion, less than a 'normal' person earning $0.000037451 billion, or $37,451, per year. Rand Paul's solution includes removing nearly all taxes on investments, including capital gains. You can change that 20% to 0%, while normal people now get charged 14.5% on their income.

And most of every developed country in the world follows a progressive tax scheme. The reason is that the more you take out of society, the more you're expected to return to it. I see no reason that this is unfair. Incredible levels of wealth inequality are generally not exactly great for the health of a country and the wealthy tend to get wealthier far faster than the rest of society tend to be able to improve their earnings. I can increasingly understand an argument against big government so perhaps one idea would be to create a public investment fund, similar to the Alaska Permanent Fund, that would return a share of all returns to all shareholders, which by right of citizenship - you would be. You simultaneously help ensure the economic health of all people in your country while also creating a public investment fund to help grow your economy or invest in longterm interests that may not have the big short to mid-term growth expectations that most private investors are seeking.

For your first point, if you chose other numbers it would work better.

To get to 20% effective federal tax, you would have to earn around $82,800 for filing single (according to a tool on TaxACT.com).

This is due to the different tax brackets and to standard deductions.

At $37,451 you've entered a greater tax bracket than the Walton's have on their $3 billion of income. The tool you're referencing is using outdated tax brackets, but is accounting for the fact we have a progressive tax scheme. It has nothing to do with deductions. In our system you pay 10% on your first $9,225, 15% on your next $28225. And then after those amounts, totalling $37450, you pay 25%+ all further income - more than the Waltons pay on their $3 billion. Considering effective taxation opens a whole new bag of worms as it's a given the Waltons are also actually paying even less than 20% on their income through a wide array of tax avoidance tricks, so I think simply comparing bracket for bracket is most reasonable.

Considering effective income taxation brings up a perhaps even more fundamental issue against Rand's flat tax. While it would undoubtedly be a huge tax break for the wealthy, including a 0% tax rate on many forms of income that are disproportionately are directed towards them, it is actually an effective tax increase on the majority of Americans. The median personal income in the US as of 2013 (the same year for the tax bracket's that site is using) is $27,851. The effective tax rate, once accounting for our progressive scheme, is 13.37% as can be verified by that tool. It'd actually be a bit lower using the latest tax brackets, but the median income has also likely changed since then.

Rand's flat tax would effectively give the rich a massive tax break, while raising taxes on the majority of normal Americans.
